items.stem: In the risk equation, increasing community capacity will:
items.answer: reduce risk
items.markingKey: reduce risk. Capacity is the denominator in risk = hazard × vulnerability / capacity.

items.stem: "Risk cannot be reduced unless the hazard is controlled." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Most risk reduction works by reducing vulnerability and increasing capacity, since hazards themselves are rarely controllable.
items.markingKey: Most risk reduction works by reducing vulnerability and increasing capacity, since hazards themselves are rarely controllable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a hazard and a disaster.
items.answer: A hazard is a potential threat from a natural event; a disaster occurs when the event causes losses that exceed the community's ability to cope.
items.markingKey: A hazard is a potential threat from a natural event; a disaster occurs when the event causes losses that exceed the community's ability to cope. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using the 2023 Al Haouz earthquake, Morocco as an example, explain rural vulnerability.
items.answer: A Mw 6.8 earthquake killed about 2,960 people, mostly in remote Atlas mountain villages of mud-brick houses. Isolation and traditional building materials raised vulnerability and delayed rescue.
items.markingKey: Context (A Mw 6.8 earthquake killed about 2,960 people, mostly in remote Atlas mountain villages of mud-brick houses.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Isolation and traditional building materials raised vulnerability and delayed rescue. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to rural vulnerability.

Index scores for two cities (0-10 scale) - City X: hazard 8, vulnerability 7, capacity 3.5; City Y: hazard 8, vulnerability 3, capacity 8.

Explain why the cities have different risk despite the same hazard.
items.answer: City X has higher vulnerability and lower capacity, so the same hazard produces about five times the risk.

items.stem: Use the Pressure and Release model to explain a named disaster.
items.answer: e.g. Haiti 2010: root causes - colonial debt, poverty, weak state; dynamic pressures - rapid urbanisation of Port-au-Prince, lack of building codes and training; unsafe conditions - unreinforced concrete housing on slopes; hazard - Mw 7.0 shallow earthquake close to the capital.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Table: deaths by age group in a coastal district after a tsunami - under 10: 38%; 10-59: 34%; 60 and over: 28%; under-10s and over-60s made up 30% of the population.

(a) Calculate the share of deaths among people under 10 and over 60. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain what this suggests about vulnerability. [6]
items.answer: (a) 38 + 28 = 66% of deaths, compared with 30% of the population. (b) Children and the elderly were more than twice as likely to die as their population share suggests, because they were less able to run, swim or climb to safety.
items.markingKey: (a) 38 + 28 = 66% of deaths, compared with 30% of the population. items.stem: "Vulnerability is more important than the physical hazard in determining disaster impacts." Discuss this statement, with reference to examples you have studied.
items.answer: Vulnerability largely explains differences in impacts, but extreme hazards can overwhelm any society.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: Haiti vs Chile 2010; PAR model shows root causes of disasters. Against / limitations: very large events overwhelm capacity even in rich countries (Tōhoku); hazard magnitude limits what preparation can achieve. options: The monetary value of damage to property, infrastructure and economic activity caused by a disaster
The number of people killed by a hazard event, often much higher in lower-income countries
The characteristics of a person or community that affect their ability to anticipate, cope with, resist and recover from a hazard
A model showing disaster as the outcome of pressures from vulnerability (root causes, dynamic pressures, unsafe conditions) meeting a hazard
items.answer: A model showing disaster as the outcome of pressures from vulnerability (root causes, dynamic pressures, unsafe conditions) meeting a hazard
items.markingKey: D. "Pressure and Release (PAR) model" is a model showing disaster as the outcome of pressures from vulnerability (root causes, dynamic pressures, unsafe conditions) meeting a hazard.

items.stem: Explain why the same magnitude of hazard can produce very different levels of risk in different places.
items.answer: Risk depends on vulnerability and capacity as well as the hazard: wealthier places with codes, preparedness and resources can reduce losses, whereas poverty, weak governance and poor housing magnify them.

items.markingKey: A1 28.0; A1 1.0; R1 comparison. R1 strategy targeting vulnerability or capacity.

items.stem: With reference to the 2023 Al Haouz earthquake, Morocco, explain how it illustrates rural vulnerability.
items.answer: A Mw 6.8 earthquake killed about 2,960 people, mostly in remote Atlas mountain villages of mud-brick houses. Isolation and traditional building materials raised vulnerability and delayed rescue.
items.markingKey: Context (A Mw 6.8 earthquake killed about 2,960 people, mostly in remote Atlas mountain villages of mud-brick houses.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Isolation and traditional building materials raised vulnerability and delayed rescue. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to rural vulnerability.

items.stem: The 2010 Haiti earthquake had a moment magnitude of 7.0 and the 2023 Al Haouz earthquake, Morocco had a magnitude of 6.8. Calculate how many times more energy was released by the first earthquake (energy increases by a factor of about 10^1.5 ≈ 31.6 per unit of magnitude).
items.answer: Energy ratio = 10^(1.5 × 0.2) ≈ 2 times

items.stem: Briefly describe the 2010 eruption of Mount Merapi, Indonesia and explain what it reveals about cultural influences on hazard perception.
items.answer: About 350 people died, including the spiritual gatekeeper Mbah Maridjan, who refused to leave. Traditional beliefs and attachment to place affected responses to warnings.
items.markingKey: Context (About 350 people died, including the spiritual gatekeeper Mbah Maridjan, who refused to leave.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Traditional beliefs and attachment to place affected responses to warnings. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to cultural influences on hazard perception.

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Index scores for two cities (0-10 scale) - City X: hazard 8, vulnerability 7, capacity 3.5; City Y: hazard 8, vulnerability 3, capacity 8.

Calculate the risk score for each city using risk = hazard × vulnerability / capacity.
items.markingKey: X: 8 × 7 / 3.5 = 16.0; Y: 8 × 3 / 8 = 3.0 Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Give one strength and one weakness of the claim that high-income countries recover more successfully from geophysical disasters than low-income countries.
items.answer: HICs usually recover faster economically, but recovery is uneven in all countries.
items.markingKey: For: insurance and government funds (Christchurch EQC). Against: Christchurch recovery still took over a decade. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Survey results from 200 residents living near a volcano: "eruption likely in next 10 years" - farmers 28 of 80; townspeople 66 of 120. "Would evacuate if ordered" - farmers 44 of 80; townspeople 102 of 120.

(a) Calculate the percentage of farmers and townspeople who would evacuate if ordered. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest reasons for the difference. [6]
items.answer: (a) Farmers 44/80 = 55%; townspeople 102/120 = 85% (b) Farmers depend on land and livestock that cannot be moved, have stronger ties to the land and may perceive lower risk; townspeople have fewer assets at risk and more access to information.
items.markingKey: (a) Farmers 44/80 = 55%; townspeople 102/120 = 85% (b) Farmers depend on land and livestock that cannot be moved, have stronger ties to the land and may perceive lower risk; townspeople have fewer assets at risk and more access to information. items.answer: Development is a key factor, but governance and the nature of the hazard are also crucial.

items.stem: A hazard becomes a disaster when:
options: its magnitude exceeds 6
it occurs at night
it exceeds the community's capacity to cope
it is recorded by satellites
items.answer: it exceeds the community's capacity to cope
items.markingKey: C. The same event can be a disaster in one place but not another.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "economic loss"?
options: The monetary value of damage to property, infrastructure and economic activity caused by a disaster
A country with gross national income per capita above the World Bank threshold (about US$14,000 in 2024)
The belief that hazards are acts of God or fate and cannot be prevented, so people accept losses
The way decisions are made and implemented by governments and institutions, including laws, enforcement and accountability
items.answer: The monetary value of damage to property, infrastructure and economic activity caused by a disaster
items.markingKey: A. "economic loss" is the monetary value of damage to property, infrastructure and economic activity caused by a disaster.

items.stem: Which response to hazards involves accepting losses as inevitable?
items.answer: Fatalism
items.markingKey: Fatalism. Other responses include adaptation, prediction and risk sharing.

items.stem: Explain how the Pressure and Release model helps explain disasters.
items.answer: It shows disasters result from vulnerability progressing from root causes (poverty, power) via dynamic pressures (rapid urbanisation, lack of training) to unsafe conditions (fragile housing), which meet a hazard; reducing these pressures "releases" the risk.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows disasters result from vulnerability progressing from root causes (poverty, power) via dynamic pressures (rapid urbanisation, lack of training) to unsafe conditions (fragile housing), which meet a hazard; reducing these pressures "releases" the risk. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why deaths from geophysical hazards are usually higher in low-income countries.
items.answer: Poor building quality and lack of enforced codes, informal settlements on hazardous land, weak warning systems, fewer emergency services and health care, and limited capacity for rescue and recovery.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Poor building quality and lack of enforced codes, informal settlements on hazardous land, weak warning systems, fewer emergency services and health care, and limited capacity for rescue and recovery. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why people may choose to live in hazardous areas.
items.answer: Economic benefits (fertile soils, tourism, geothermal energy), lack of alternatives, family and cultural ties, low perception of risk or optimism, and belief that technology will protect them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Economic benefits (fertile soils, tourism, geothermal energy), lack of alternatives, family and cultural ties, low perception of risk or optimism, and belief that technology will protect them. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between capacity and vulnerability.
items.answer: Vulnerability is the susceptibility of people to harm; capacity is the resources and abilities that allow them to resist and recover - risk rises with vulnerability and falls with capacity.
items.markingKey: Vulnerability is the susceptibility of people to harm; capacity is the resources and abilities that allow them to resist and recover - risk rises with vulnerability and falls with capacity. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between relative economic losses and absolute economic losses.
items.answer: Absolute losses are the total cost in money and are usually highest in HICs; relative losses compare costs with GDP and are often highest in LICs.
items.markingKey: Absolute losses are the total cost in money and are usually highest in HICs; relative losses compare costs with GDP and are often highest in LICs. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between NGOs and governments.
items.answer: Governments set and enforce laws, fund infrastructure and lead national response; NGOs are independent, often work at community level, and provide relief, training and advocacy.
items.markingKey: Governments set and enforce laws, fund infrastructure and lead national response; NGOs are independent, often work at community level, and provide relief, training and advocacy. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

Calculate the share of deaths among people under 10 and over 60.
items.answer: 38 + 28 = 66% of deaths, compared with 30% of the population.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the 2010 Haiti earthquake shows disasters in low-income countries.
items.answer: Over 100,000 people died and about 1.5 million were made homeless, with losses estimated at about 120% of GDP. Poverty, weak government and poor building quality magnified impacts.
items.markingKey: Context (Over 100,000 people died and about 1.5 million were made homeless, with losses estimated at about 120% of GDP.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With reference to the 2010 Haiti earthquake, explain how it illustrates vulnerability in disasters.
items.answer: A Mw 7.0 earthquake near Port-au-Prince killed an estimated 100,000-316,000 people. Poverty, weak governance and unreinforced buildings magnified the impact.
items.markingKey: Context (A Mw 7.0 earthquake near Port-au-Prince killed an estimated 100,000-316,000 people.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Table: economic losses as % of GDP - Haiti 2010: 120%; Nepal 2015: 33%; Chile 2010: 18%; Japan (Tōhoku) 2011: about 4%.

(a) Describe the pattern shown. [4]

items.answer: (a) Losses relative to GDP were highest in the lowest-income countries (Haiti, Nepal) and lowest in Japan, the richest. (b) Its losses (about US$235 billion) involved very high-value infrastructure, housing and industry, plus the Fukushima nuclear disaster.

(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain why staged alert levels are useful. [6]
items.answer: (a) 7 June to 15 June = 8 days (b) They communicate increasing risk simply, allowing progressive evacuation and avoiding the costs of evacuating too early.
